title: The horse has been made redundant
lines: A car is a sofa with wheels, a controlled fire, and a monthly payment. Somehow we decided children should grow up wanting one.
And the electric version replaces the fire with chemistry, magnets, and arguments about charging.
How did we get from a horse pulling a box to a box that tells us our phone needs updating?
By solving one problem at a time, then discovering three new ones. Today we follow the history, open up the machinery, and explain what actually makes cars move, turn and stop.
Finally, a history lesson with torque.

title: 1769: A kettle applies for a driving licence
lines: In seventeen sixty-nine, Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot tested a steam-powered vehicle intended for military hauling. A larger version followed. Early cars did not begin with petrol.
They began with someone looking at a kettle and asking, can this tow artillery?
Fuel heats water in a boiler. Steam pressure pushes pistons. Mechanical linkages turn that back-and-forth movement into wheel motion.
But boilers were heavy, and starting involved raising steam. Keeping water and fire under control added work. Replacing the horse did not automatically make travel convenient.
The horse could at least start without preheating. Although its emissions were also noticeable.

visual.title: Steam propulsion: heat outside the working cylinder
visual.source: Musée des Arts et Métiers: Cugnot
visual.caption: Simplified explanatory sequence; not a scale drawing.

note: 1769 refers to the prototype; the surviving larger fardier is dated 1770–1771. Do not repeat the unverified first-car-crash story.

title: 1876–1886: Bring the fire indoors
lines: Internal combustion moved the burning into the engine itself. Instead of making steam elsewhere, burning fuel and air creates hot gases that push a piston directly.
The fire has moved from an external contractor to a permanent member of staff.

In eighteen seventy-six, Nicolaus Otto developed a practical four-stroke compressed-charge engine. In eighteen eighty-six, Carl Benz applied for the patent associated with his purpose-built petrol motor car.
Three wheels, one cylinder, and absolutely no argument about where to put the touchscreen.
Benz is a key milestone, not the sole inventor of everything automotive. Steam vehicles preceded him; Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach were also developing lightweight engines and motor vehicles.
History has a whole workshop. The thumbnail only has room for one moustache.

visual.title: Two major milestones, not one inventor of everything
visual.caption: Other inventors and earlier steam vehicles also contributed.

title: 1888: Bertha takes the prototype outside
lines: In eighteen eighty-eight, Bertha Benz took a Benz motor car on a journey of more than a hundred kilometres, with her two sons.
An ambitious family outing. Especially when roadside assistance is just whichever son looks less tired.
She travelled from Mannheim to Pforzheim and obtained fuel from a pharmacy along the way. This helped demonstrate that the invention could make a substantial journey.
One bottle of cough syrup, please. And a tank of whatever the carriage is drinking.
That is our joke, not a historical quotation. The important point is that a working machine also needs fuel supply, repairs and public confidence.
The road test mattered as much as the drawing board. Literally taking the idea for a spin.

title: Under the bonnet: The four-stroke dance
lines: Explain the petrol engine without saying, the engine engines.
First: intake. The piston moves down and the intake valve opens, letting air in. Depending on the design, fuel mixes with that air before entering or is injected directly into the cylinder.
Second: compression. The piston moves up with the valves closed, squeezing the charge into a smaller space.
Like packing a suitcase, except the suitcase is about to become extremely enthusiastic.
Third: power. A timed spark starts combustion. The hot gases expand and push the piston down.
Fourth: exhaust. The exhaust valve opens and the rising piston pushes spent gases out. Then the sequence repeats.
Breathe in, squeeze, push, breathe out. The engine has a more consistent workout routine than I do.
Four piston strokes take two crankshaft revolutions. It is controlled combustion; destructive knocking is not the goal.

visual.title: Four-stroke spark-ignition engine
nodes: POWER: burning gases push piston down
visual.caption: Simplified cycle. Actual valve and ignition timing vary.

title: Pistons, crankshafts and the engine orchestra
lines: The piston goes up and down. The wheels go round. Who translates?
A connecting rod joins the piston to an offset crank on the crankshaft. That mechanism converts reciprocating motion into rotation. A flywheel helps smooth the pulses.
A translator fluent in both boing and spin.
The camshaft opens valves in step with the crankshaft, commonly through a belt or chain drive. A typical four-stroke camshaft turns once for every two crankshaft turns.
Multiple cylinders deliver their power strokes at different times. Displacement is their combined swept volume, not a direct horsepower score. Breathing, speed, combustion and boost also matter.
So a two-litre engine is a volume measurement, not how much petrol it drinks with lunch.

visual.title: From piston motion to useful rotation
visual.caption: Displacement is swept cylinder volume, not fuel consumption.

title: Air, fuel and a very punctual spark
lines: Does pressing the accelerator pour more petrol into the fire?
In a conventional petrol engine, the throttle helps control incoming air. Fuel delivery must match. Older carburettors use pressure differences in flowing air to draw and mix fuel.
Modern injection meters fuel more precisely. Port injection sprays before the intake valve; direct injection sprays into the cylinder. An ignition coil supplies the high voltage for the spark.
A carburettor is a mechanical recipe. Injection adds a very fussy digital chef.
Too much or too little fuel changes combustion. Timing matters too: ignition is arranged so the pressure rise does useful work as the piston moves.
The engine wants dinner and an appointment, not just a bucket of enthusiasm.

visual.title: Petrol combustion needs coordination
visual.caption: Conceptual control sequence, not a repair procedure.

title: Starting and charging: Two different electrical jobs
lines: If an engine must turn to run, what turns it before it is running?
In a conventional petrol car, the battery powers a starter motor. It turns the engine until combustion can sustain operation; then the starter disengages.
The engine needs someone to get it out of bed. Relatable.
Once running, the engine commonly drives an alternator. It supplies electrical power and replenishes the small vehicle battery through a regulated charging system.
That is not the same as an electric car’s large traction battery. Some hybrids also use different starter-generator arrangements.
Starter gets the party going. Alternator keeps the lights on. Neither is powered by the confidence of the person turning the key.

visual.title: Conventional combustion-car electrics
nodes: Alternator supplies power and charges battery
visual.caption: Typical arrangement; hybrids and integrated starter-generators can differ.

title: Oil and coolant: The unglamorous heroes
lines: If burning fuel makes motion, why not just make everything hotter?

Because engines have temperature limits. In a liquid-cooled design, coolant carries heat from the engine to a radiator, where it passes to the surrounding air. A thermostat helps regulate circulation.
The radiator is the engine politely opening a window.
Oil does a different job: it forms lubricating films between moving surfaces, reduces wear and also helps carry heat and contamination. Coolant and oil are not interchangeable beverages.
And the metal rings around the piston?
They help seal combustion pressure and control oil on the cylinder wall. The whole machine depends on clearances, seals and lubrication, not just dramatic flames.
So the engine is mostly tiny gaps being managed extremely seriously.

visual.title: Keeping an engine alive
visual.source: DENSO cooling guide; Briggs & Stratton glossary
visual.caption: Different systems cooperate; oil and coolant are separate circuits.

title: The gearbox: A bicycle lesson with invoices
lines: Why does a running engine not stall whenever the car stops?
A manual car can disconnect the engine from the gearbox using its clutch. Reconnecting progressively lets the engine bring the car into motion.
Gears trade rotational speed for torque, which means turning force. A low gear multiplies wheel torque while the wheels turn more slowly relative to the engine. Think of climbing on a bicycle.
The easier pedalling gear. My legs understand engineering when there is a hill.
Higher gears suit faster travel with fewer engine revolutions per wheel turn. Gears do not create free power; real transmissions also lose some energy as heat.
Power is how quickly work is done. For a rotating shaft, it depends on torque and rotational speed together. A large torque number alone does not describe the whole performance.

visual.title: A manual drivetrain
nodes: Gear ratio trades speed for torque
visual.caption: Schematic. Ratios and layouts differ between vehicles.

title: The differential: Why corners require diplomacy
lines: Both driven wheels get power. Why not bolt them to one solid shaft?
During a turn, the outside wheel travels farther than the inside wheel. A differential transmits torque while allowing different wheel speeds.
Like two friends walking around a roundabout. The outside friend needs more steps and probably more snacks.

An ordinary open differential has a traction limitation: if one wheel can support very little torque, that can limit useful torque at the other. Limited-slip and locking designs address this differently.
A common rack-and-pinion system converts steering-wheel rotation into sideways rack movement that turns the road wheels. Hydraulic or electric assistance reduces driver effort.
Power steering: because parking should not be an upper-body qualification exam.

visual.title: Turn without making the tyres fight
visual.caption: Separate functions: steering changes direction; differential allows speed difference.

title: 1897: Diesel does ignition differently
lines: Meanwhile, another engine branch developed. Rudolf Diesel and the Augsburg engineering works produced a successful diesel engine in eighteen ninety-seven.
A conventional diesel compresses air strongly enough to heat it. Fuel is then injected into that hot compressed air and ignites without a spark plug initiating the normal combustion event.
The petrol engine needs a spark. The diesel engine brings its own heated discussion.
Glow plugs can help cold starting; they are not spark plugs. Diesel designs can be efficient, but soot and nitrogen oxides require attention. Diesel development did not instantly replace petrol cars.
Two branches of the family tree. Both capable of expensive noises.

visual.title: Compression ignition
visual.source: MAN history; DOE: combustion engine basics
visual.caption: Simplified diesel ignition, not the full four-stroke sequence.

title: Around 1900: Three engines enter the chat
lines: Around nineteen hundred, the road was not a petrol-only club. Steam, battery-electric and petrol vehicles competed.
Electric cars were not invented when phones started losing headphone sockets?

No. Electric vehicles offered quiet operation and avoided hand-cranking. Steam had its own strengths, but heating up and managing water could be inconvenient. Batteries limited range and charging opportunities.
So the argument about how to power a car is older than most car companies.

Petrol cars gained advantages from falling prices, refuelling infrastructure and improved convenience. The electric starter, introduced on Cadillac in nineteen twelve, helped remove the hand-cranking ordeal.
Humanity invented an electric motor so it could more conveniently start its non-electric motor. Beautifully complicated.

visual.title: Early propulsion rivals
visual.source: US Department of Energy: EV history
visual.caption: Alternatives coexisted; this is not a strict replacement sequence.

title: 1908–1913: The invention becomes a production problem
lines: Ford introduced the Model T in nineteen-oh-eight. In nineteen thirteen, its team developed moving assembly-line production at Highland Park. Ford did not invent the car.
He helped invent the situation where everybody could eventually complain about traffic.
Instead of workers repeatedly travelling around a stationary vehicle, work came past organised stations. Standardised parts and specialised tasks improved throughput.
The Library of Congress describes assembly time falling from twelve and a half hours to ninety-three minutes. That is seven hundred and fifty minutes versus ninety-three on our chart.
The car was not driving faster. The factory was.
This compares reported assembly time, not the time to mine steel and manufacture every component. Lower costs expanded access, though affordability was never universal.

visual.title: Reported Model T assembly time
visual.source: Library of Congress: Ford assembly-line history
visual.caption: 12.5 hours × 60 = 750 minutes. Assembly time, not total manufacturing time.

title: Bodies, layouts and the disappearing third pedal
lines: Through the early twentieth century, cars became more integrated machines. Many used bodies mounted on separate frames; unitised structures instead make much of the body carry structural loads.
The difference between putting a house on scaffolding and designing the house to support itself.
Engine placement and driven wheels varied. Front-wheel drive groups propulsion near the front; rear-wheel drive sends power rearward. Packaging, weight distribution and cost all influence the choice.
For the nineteen-forty model year, Oldsmobile offered the Hydra-Matic automatic. Later automatic designs often used torque converters; that original Hydra-Matic used a fluid coupling.
Important distinction. History also needs its fluids checked.
Automatic gear changes reduced the driver's workload. Today there are several approaches, including planetary automatics, dual-clutch systems and continuously variable transmissions.

visual.title: Beyond the engine
nodes: Layout packages engine and driven wheels
visual.caption: These are design choices, not a ranking of every vehicle.

title: Automatic, dual-clutch and CVT: Three ways to shift
lines: Automatic is one gearbox design, right?

It describes who handles the shifting, not one universal mechanism. A common automatic uses a torque converter to transfer engine power through moving fluid, with gearsets and clutches providing different ratios.
A fluid handshake instead of my left foot negotiating with a clutch pedal.
A dual-clutch transmission divides gears between two clutches, commonly odd and even sets, so the next gear can be prepared before the handover.
A belt or chain CVT changes its effective pulley diameters to vary the ratio continuously. It need not jump between a fixed set of steps.
Stairs versus a ramp. Both get you upstairs, with different complaints from enthusiasts.
And an e-CVT label on some hybrids can refer to a different power-split system, not that belt-and-pulley design. Similar names do not guarantee identical machinery.

visual.title: Automatic is a category, not one mechanism
nodes: Belt or chain CVT varies pulley ratio
visual.source: ZF transmission guides; Nissan CVT documentation
visual.caption: Conceptual comparison. Hybrid e-CVT systems can work differently.

title: Tyres and suspension: Negotiating with the road
lines: Could engineers solve bad roads by making the seats extremely fluffy?
Comfort matters, but so does keeping tyres in contact with the road. Springs support the vehicle and let wheels move over bumps. Dampers control the resulting bouncing.
Springs are the enthusiastic friend. Dampers are the friend saying, please calm down.
Tyres provide the grip for accelerating, steering and braking. Michelin filed its radial-tyre patent in nineteen forty-six, an important step in tyre construction.
In a radial design, casing cords run across the tyre from bead to bead, with belts supporting the tread. Construction, rubber, pressure and road conditions all affect behaviour.
A powerful engine still negotiates with the road through rubber. Expensive horsepower, meet wet roundabout.

visual.title: Road contact is a system
nodes: Tyres transmit forces to the road
visual.caption: A radial tyre is a construction type, not a guarantee of grip.

title: Brakes: Turning urgency into heat
lines: The brakes destroy speed. Where does the speed go?
Friction brakes convert much of the car's kinetic energy into heat. In a common hydraulic system, pedal force creates fluid pressure that operates brakes at the wheels.
Disc brakes clamp pads against a rotating disc. Drum brakes press shoes against the inside of a drum. The tyres must still grip the road to slow the car.
So the car warms its dinner plates to prevent us becoming a collision.
At the same mass, kinetic energy depends on speed squared. At thirty kilometres per hour, call it one unit. At sixty, it is four units. At ninety, nine.
Double the speed, quadruple the energy. Physics charges surge pricing.
This is an energy comparison, not a measured stopping-distance chart. Reaction time, grip, gradient and the braking system also matter.

visual.title: Same mass: kinetic energy rises with speed squared
visual.caption: 30 km/h baseline = 1. Not stopping distances or crash-test results.

title: 1959: The passenger is part of the engineering
lines: Early advertising concentrated on going. When did we start worrying about surviving the stopping?
Safety developed through many contributions. In nineteen fifty-nine, Volvo introduced Nils Bohlin's modern three-point belt. It restrains the torso and pelvis together.
A diagonal strap doing more useful work than most motivational slogans.
A crumple zone absorbs energy through controlled deformation while the passenger compartment aims to preserve survival space. Restraints help manage the occupant's deceleration.
Airbags supplement seat belts; they do not replace them. Simply making every part of a car rigid would not make the people inside invulnerable.
The goal is not a car that wins an argument with a wall. It is occupants who get another day.

visual.title: Crash protection works together
visual.caption: Conceptual roles, not the timing of a particular crash.

title: 1967 onward: The engine gets a nervous system
lines: Bosch put its Jetronic electronic petrol injection into series production in nineteen sixty-seven. Electronics increasingly helped control what had been a largely mechanical balancing act.
The engine got a brain. Mine still forgets why it entered the kitchen.
Sensors measure conditions such as airflow or pressure, temperature and crankshaft position. A controller uses this information to command fuel delivery and ignition.
Oxygen sensing in the exhaust can provide feedback for mixture control. Electronic accelerator pedals send a request to the controller rather than always tugging a cable directly.
The accelerator is now an email marked urgent.
Precise control can improve starting, drivability, efficiency and emissions. The trade-off is more components and software to understand when something goes wrong.

visual.title: Electronic engine control
nodes: Actuators adjust fuel, air and ignition
visual.source: Bosch: electronics history and engine management
visual.caption: Feedback continues repeatedly; this diagram shows one simplified pass.

title: 1970s: The exhaust becomes everyone’s business
lines: The twentieth century made cars common. It also made breathing beside a busy road a questionable hobby.
Oil shocks and air-quality concerns increased pressure for economy and cleaner exhaust. In the United States, catalytic converters became common on new cars from the nineteen-seventy-five model year.
A catalyst helps chemical reactions occur. Modern three-way converters tackle carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons and nitrogen oxides when operating under the right conditions.
An exhaust cleanup crew. Not a magical pipe that turns every bad thing into butterflies.
Correct. It does not eliminate carbon dioxide. Pollution controls, efficiency improvements and fuel changes addressed different problems, and countries adopted them at different times.
Cleaner exhaust and zero environmental impact are very different claims. One fits a laboratory. The other fits an advertisement.

visual.title: Three-way catalytic conversion: simplified targets
visual.caption: Does not remove all emissions or eliminate CO₂.

title: The turbo: Your exhaust gets a second job
lines: More power means we simply make the engine bigger?
Not necessarily. A turbocharger uses energy in the exhaust flow to spin a turbine. A shaft connects it to a compressor that pushes more air into the engine.
The exhaust was leaving work. Management has found it another task.
More air allows more fuel to burn when the engine is designed and controlled for it. An intercooler reduces the temperature of the compressed intake air.
Boost control limits pressure. The system adds heat and mechanical demands, and some combinations have a delay in response called turbo lag. It is not free energy.
A conventional supercharger is driven mechanically by the engine rather than by an exhaust turbine. Similar aim, different way of paying the energy bill.

visual.title: Turbocharging
nodes: Engine burns a larger controlled charge
visual.caption: Air and exhaust remain separate streams; the shaft transfers mechanical power.

title: 1983 and beyond: There is more than one national story
lines: So car history is Germany inventing, America mass-producing, then everyone else buying?
That leaves out a very large part of the map. Production, design and manufacturing methods developed across many countries, including major European and Japanese industries.
In India, the first Maruti eight hundred reached its first customer in December nineteen eighty-three. The company began as a government and Suzuki joint venture.
A significant chapter in Indian motoring, not the first car ever seen in India.
Exactly. Different markets needed different combinations of price, space, fuel economy and serviceability. Progress was not simply making every car larger.
Sometimes progress was fitting the family budget into a smaller parking space. The relatives still requested more legroom.
note: Broad international context is not a claim that one country invented affordability. Avoid invented sales or market-share figures.

title: 1978–1995: Brakes learn to think in milliseconds
lines: Another strand matured alongside those changes: electronic safety. Bosch's production-ready electronic anti-lock braking system arrived in nineteen seventy-eight; electronic stability control followed in nineteen ninety-five with Mercedes-Benz.
We finally gave the brakes permission to interrupt bad decisions.
Anti-lock braking uses wheel-speed information to modulate pressure when wheels approach locking. Keeping wheels rolling helps retain steering control during hard braking.
Stability control compares the driver's intended direction with the vehicle's motion. It can brake individual wheels and reduce engine torque to counter a developing skid.
An invisible referee for the car's dance moves.
But tyres still have limited grip. Electronics cannot cancel ice, excessive speed or the laws of physics.

visual.title: Electronic braking and stability
visual.caption: Related systems with different functions; not a three-step emergency procedure.

title: 1997: The hybrid stops choosing sides
lines: Petrol versus electric. Can the car simply refuse to pick a team?
That is one reason hybrids are interesting. The Toyota Prius launched in Japan in nineteen ninety-seven, a landmark mass-produced hybrid passenger car. Hybrid experiments existed much earlier.
A hybrid combines a combustion engine, electric motor and battery. Depending on the design, the engine can drive the wheels, generate electricity, or do both through the powertrain.
A group project where the participants actually have different useful skills.
A conventional hybrid does not plug into the grid. Its stored electrical energy comes from the engine and recovered braking energy. A plug-in hybrid can also charge externally.
So self-charging does not mean the car discovered a loophole in thermodynamics.

visual.title: Hybrid energy sources
visual.caption: Architectures vary. A conventional hybrid is not a plug-in hybrid.

title: Regeneration: A refund, not free money
lines: How does slowing down charge a battery?
The drivetrain can make an electric motor act as a generator. Taking energy from the moving car creates a resisting torque, while some of that energy returns electrically to the battery.
So friction braking turns the receipt into heat. Regeneration gets part of the purchase refunded.
Exactly: part. Conversion losses remain. Battery temperature, charge level and power limits can restrict recovery. Ordinary friction brakes still have important work to do.
Could I accelerate and brake repeatedly to make extra electricity?
No. Every round trip loses energy. Regeneration recovers some energy you already spent; it does not manufacture a bonus supply.
Physics has rejected my cashback scheme.

visual.title: Regenerative braking
visual.source: DOE AFDC: hybrid and electric vehicles
visual.caption: Recovery is limited and incomplete; friction brakes remain necessary.

title: 2008–2010: Electric cars make a louder quiet entrance
lines: Battery-electric cars returned to wider attention as batteries, power electronics and manufacturing developed. This was a comeback, not a brand-new invention.
The early electric car had been waiting for a very long software update.
The original Tesla Roadster entered production in two thousand eight. The Nissan Leaf followed in two thousand ten as a major attempt to bring modern battery-electric motoring to a wider market.
One made electric performance conspicuous. The other looked more ready for groceries.
Neither company invented the electric motor or the electric car. These were milestones in a much longer story involving many firms and researchers.
And the horse, observing all this from a field, remained comfortably unsubscribed.

title: Inside an EV: Magnets replace the combustion party
lines: In a typical modern battery-electric drivetrain, the battery supplies direct current. An inverter controls electrical power for the traction motor.
Controlled currents in the stationary part, the stator, create magnetic fields. Their interaction with the rotor produces turning force. Motor designs differ in how they create those magnetic fields.
A carefully timed magnetic dance, instead of pistons having a heated disagreement.
Many electric cars use a single fixed reduction ratio because their motors work across a broad speed range. They still have gears; some designs use more than one ratio.
Fewer gear changes does not mean no engineering.
Right. Bearings, reduction gears, a differential, cooling and control electronics still matter. A small auxiliary electrical system also powers accessories and control functions.

visual.title: Typical battery-electric drivetrain
visual.source: DOE AFDC; Tesla Roadster technical manual
visual.caption: Simplified architecture; motor and drivetrain designs vary.

title: Inside the battery: Chemistry, not bottled lightning
lines: What actually travels through a lithium-ion battery?
During discharge, lithium ions move inside the cell through the electrolyte, while electrons travel through the external circuit to do useful work. Recharging reverses the overall process.
Two coordinated routes. The ions stay inside; the electrons take the working commute.

Cells are combined into a pack. A battery-management system monitors conditions, and thermal management helps keep operation within suitable temperatures. Different battery chemistries trade cost, energy density and other properties.
So a battery pack is less a giant AA battery and more a closely supervised apartment complex.
And capacity and power are different. Kilowatt-hours measure energy stored; kilowatts measure the rate of energy transfer. Think tank size versus how quickly fuel can flow.

visual.title: Battery essentials
visual.caption: Ion and electron paths differ. Values depend on battery design.

title: Charging: The last ten percent has questions
lines: Why does a huge charger number not guarantee a tiny charging time?
On an AC connection, the car's onboard charger converts alternating current into DC for the battery. With DC fast charging, that conversion happens outside the car.
Actual power depends on the charger, vehicle limits, battery temperature and state of charge. Charging commonly slows as the battery gets fuller.
Like packing the last clothes into a suitcase, except the suitcase has sensors and refuses to negotiate.
Range also changes with speed, weather, terrain and heating or cooling demand. Charging infrastructure matters just as fuel infrastructure mattered to Bertha Benz.
The pharmacy joke has become a charger-location app. History really does enjoy a callback.

visual.title: Charging depends on the whole system
nodes: AC: onboard conversion; DC: external conversion
Conditions affect charging and usable range
visual.source: DOE AFDC: charging and EV components
visual.caption: A charger’s advertised maximum is not a constant charging rate.

title: Efficiency: The air also sends an invoice
lines: If the electric motor is efficient, can we stop worrying about energy?
No. Any car needs energy to accelerate, climb, overcome tyre losses and push air aside. At otherwise similar conditions, aerodynamic drag force grows roughly with speed squared.
So driving faster makes the air increasingly uncooperative.
An electric car has no combustion tailpipe emissions, but manufacturing, battery production and electricity generation still have impacts. A life-cycle comparison includes those stages.
The electricity mix, vehicle size and use affect that comparison. Zero tailpipe emissions does not mean zero impact from everything involved in making and using the vehicle.
The exhaust pipe disappeared. The need to count honestly did not.

visual.title: Follow the energy and the impacts
nodes: Energy moves the car and overcomes losses
Manufacturing also uses energy and materials
Electricity or fuel supply adds impacts
visual.source: NASA drag equation; DOE AFDC emissions
visual.caption: Life-cycle impact and tailpipe emissions are different measures.

title: The software era: Assistance is not a chauffeur
lines: Now the car can steer, brake and complain about lane markings. Has the driver become decorative?
Not with ordinary driver-assistance systems. Cameras, radar and other sensors can support features such as adaptive cruise control or lane assistance. Capabilities and limitations vary.

At Level Two automation, the system can control steering and speed together, but the driver must remain engaged and supervise. That is different from a system authorised to operate without a driver under defined conditions.
The label assistant is doing important work in that sentence.
Software also manages powertrains, diagnostics and many comfort functions. But a confident dashboard graphic is not proof that a car understands every situation.
We started by removing the horse. Let us not remove common sense as an optional extra.

visual.title: Know who is responsible
nodes: Driver responsibility depends on the system
visual.caption: Level 2 requires active driver supervision. No universal self-driving claim.

title: Two centuries, one ongoing group project
lines: Let me check the journey. Steam moved the carriage. Petrol made compact combustion practical. Production lines made cars easier to manufacture. Better chassis, tyres and brakes made them more usable.
Safety engineering protected people. Electronics refined control. Hybrids combined power sources, and modern batteries helped electric cars return to a much bigger stage.
Underneath all of it: store energy, convert it into torque, transmit it, find grip, and steer. Then slow down without ruining everyone's afternoon.
And every solution brings trade-offs: cost, weight, convenience, resources, pollution, safety and the space a car occupies. There is no single invention that settles every question.
So the history of cars is a centuries-long engineering group project.
Yes. With unusually expensive group members.
Still has four-wheel drive. Terrible Bluetooth.
